step1_summary: Chief complaint: Soreness and cracked skin on fingers/hands (mainly palms)
- Onset: ~3–4 months ago, after changing jobs
- Severity: Now painful, interfering with work/ADLs
- Aggravating factors: Scratching (leads to bleeding), using cleaning chemicals at work
- Alleviating factors: Tried emollient (E45) and antihistamines without improvement
- Character: Itchy (intermittent), painful, cracked, occasionally bleeds if scratched
- Distribution: Mainly hands (palms), some mild dryness on legs
- Family: Diabetes (no known skin conditions, asthma, or bowel problems in family)
- Social: Housekeeper (cleaning in hotels), recent job change; often does not wear gloves

V: Peripheral vascular disease: Diabetes can predispose, but no evidence of color changes, ulceration, or pulses loss.
I: Contact dermatitis (irritant/contact): Supported by occupational exposure to cleaning chemicals, cracked/itchy hands, and effect on palms.
Eczema (atopic/contact): History of dry skin elsewhere, pruritic, and cracked lesions.
Fungal infection (tinea manuum): Chronic hand rash possible, but classic features (annular, central clearing, scaling, involvement of one hand) not described.
N: Cutaneous malignancy (very unlikely): No nodules, ulcerations, or chronic non-healing lesions described.
D: Diabetic-related skin changes (xerosis): Diabetes can cause increased dryness/pruritus, but lacks inflammation described here.
Vitamin deficiency (e.g., B3/niacin—pellagra): Unlikely without other systemic findings (glossitis, diarrhea, dementia).
I2: Iatrogenic: No new medications; metformin rarely associated with skin reactions.
Intoxication: No mention of exposure to toxins beyond cleaning chemicals.
C: Congenital ichthyosis: No childhood history or generalized involvement—unlikely.
A: Allergic contact dermatitis: Could be allergy to products, but more likely irritant given chronicity and occupation.
Autoimmune (e.g., psoriasis): Palmar psoriasis possible with fissuring, but no clear evidence of plaques/silvery scale/history.
T: Trauma: Chronic mechanical trauma possible (hands at work), but pattern and chronicity fit irritant dermatitis more.
E: Hypothyroidism: Can cause dryness, but no systemic features or exam findings.
Diabetic-related skin changes/Xerosis: As above under D.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Chronic hand dermatitis in a housekeeper with frequent exposure to cleaning chemicals, not wearing gloves, and the time course corresponding with a new job. Symptoms (itch, soreness, cracks, worse with exposure, minimal response to emollients/antihistamines) support irritant mechanism.
supporting_evidence: Works as a housekeeper using cleaning agents without regular glove use
Painful, cracked, itchy skin; worse over time
opposing_evidence: Mild dryness on legs (not hands only), but this is not severe

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Clinical features could fit allergic as well as irritant contact dermatitis; occupational exposure; although time course and lack of prior eczema/history make irritant somewhat more likely.
supporting_evidence: Hand dermatitis corresponding with use of cleaning products
Symptoms improve with avoidance (time off work)
opposing_evidence: No personal or family history of other atopic disease
Not all areas in contact with products are equally affected; more likely irritant

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Some generalized dryness and pruritus, but lacks a history of atopy (no childhood eczema, asthma, or family history), and hands are predominantly affected.
opposing_evidence: No prior or family history of atopy or eczema

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Chronicity could fit; but no description of scaling, annular lesions, or involvement of only one hand; no mention of involvement of feet.
opposing_evidence: No description of scaling, classic fungal pattern
No mention of involvement elsewhere or predisposing factors

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Chronic, fissured, dry palms can signal psoriasis; but lacks history of plaque psoriasis, silvery scales, or family history.
opposing_evidence: No history/finding of plaques, nail changes, or personal/family history of psoriasis
